questions.answer:
Quite hard tbh. The hard part is not finding a room, but rather convincing the landlord to shorten the lease from the more normal 10-month one to a 4-5 month one (without them significantly raising the cost!) - I browsed through a bunch of Facebook adds and narrowly avoided being scammed.
I recommend either getting help from Cornell (more expensive) or use the Cornell-certified website for housing (forgot the name, it will come up in early orientation)
If you are going before 2028 you can also shoot me an email on Bertil.loessing@
gmail.com
and I might be able to put you into contact with a few Cornell students who know the housing deal campus and can help you find a room with american students (no promises).

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Try to find housing around collegetown or just below west campus for easy acces to daily needs and nightly beers. Collegetown is not very cozy or nice but it's very convenient - whereas university ave. below west campus will put you within walking distance to downtown Ithaca which I found quite charming and twin peaks-esque.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
Very easy. Just a website. It does, however, open later for exchange students meaning that some courses may get filled up before you get a chance to register - to get around this if you really want a specific course, especially (and maybe only) if you are in the humanities like me, you can email the prof. and explain your interest. It worked every time for me. 

Also, make sure to take advantage of 'shopping week' in which you can try different classes before you decide your schedule finally - this Is also a good time to approach and grease the prof. if the class is 'full'.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
Did you take BA or MA classes while you were on exchange *
Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
BA courses are generally 'mixed' between different majors - sometimes the composition of a literature class will be 60% non comp. lit. or lit. majors. While it encourages transdisciplinarity and cultivation of broader academic interests among students, it also significantly lowers the level of the class, often spiralling into purely opinionated discussion of vague topics without any theoretical ground - a frustrating experience when coming from the more structured discussions taking place in UCPH. At the same time however, the prof.'s seem to not really lower the level of teaching and lecturing which means that in some classrooms effectively 5 people are getting the point.

To avoid the worst of these mixed classrooms you should look for courses with prerequisites (if you don't have them yourself but feel confident in the material, just talk with the prof.), and look for courses that are cross listed between the BA and MA.

Or, alternatively, just apply for MA courses with the phd. students - I had one such class at it was amazing. I guess it depends on one's academic ambitions and goals for exchange, but if you feel like being challenged it's a great option.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: smaller classes (5-10 people), discussion based, close readings, closer and more personal relations with professors, higher course load (readings + assignments).
